Comments on the Psychodynamics of Interaction

Joseph Sandler Ph.D., M.D., LL.D.

Joseph Sandler

35 Circus Road
London NW8 9JG

Joseph Sandler  

One of the major theoretical issues in considering processes of interaction is the question of whether it is appropriate to use a one-person or two-person frame of reference. This is a complicated issue and one that cannot be answered simply by saying that the psychoanalytic model of the mind is a one-person model on the grounds that all information arising from the outside does so as mental representations of one sort or another. Further, it could be said that the essence of the psychoanalytic point of view is that these representations, and all our feelings, are profoundly affected by what arises from the inside. In a paper some years ago (Sandler, 1983), I suggested that the theoretical models, theories, or schemata used by psychoanalysts are not fully integrated with one another and that there were significant differences between our private psychoanalytic theories and what I called the “public” or “official” theories of psychoanalysis. I suggested that the complex private preconscious working model of the psychoanalyst—essentially a set of not very well integrated part-theories—had an important advantage over the public or “official” ones in that “such a loosely-jointed theory … allows developments in psychoanalytic theory to take place without necessarily causing radical disruptions …” (p. 36).

Dr. Sandler is Emeritus Professor of Psychoanalysis and Co-Director of the Psychoanalysis Unit at the University College London, and Training and Supervising Analyst, British Psychoanalytical Society.

Paper presented at a panel on “Interaction,” at the meeting of the American Psychoanalytic Association, New York, December 21, 1991.

Evelyne Schwaber MD

Evelyne Schwaber

4 Welland Road
Brookline, MA 02146

Evelyne Schwaber  

I believe that there is a fundamental conceptual difficulty in the clinical term interaction. The Concordance (Guttman, 1984) indicates that in the Standard Edition Freud's use refers just to the interaction between different psychical agencies. It is not listed in Moore and Fine's Psychoanalytic Terms and Concepts (1990) nor in Laplanche and Pontalis's The Language of Psycho-Analysis (1973). Nonetheless, it speaks to a phenomenon between analyst and analysand central to our understanding of the analytic process and intrinsic to what ensues within it—a term with which we need to grapple. It is a truism—we participate in that which we also observe. And we can note that this observation itself is integral to our interaction. This participant-observer view has been increasingly recognized and explicated, particularly with the shift away from a blank screen model of the analytic exchange. It has more regularly entered the “mainstream” literature associated with the “traditional,” or ego-psychological, view (Boesky, 1990; Gill, 1982; Renik, 1993; Schwaber, 1981, 1983, 1992a, b)

Dr. Schwaber is Training and Supervising Analyst, Psychoanalytic Institute of New England, East; Faculty, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute.

Epilogue

Eloise Agger D.S.W.

Eloise Agger

Eloise Agger  

F. Scott Fitzgerald is reported to have described America as a place where there are no second acts. You have been present to enjoy our second act. In terms of metapsychology, both sets of essays on How the Analyst's Work Shapes the Analyst have attested not to radical alternatives to practice based on classical psychoanalytic theory but to a theory of accommodations to it. We have assimilated lessons from past teachers, such as from Hans Loewald (1986):

Transference and countertransference may become indistinguishable: in pronounced instances we are no longer dealing with “significant others” and their transference and our countertransference, but the two would-be individuals become enmeshed in a psychic force field with no boundaries [p. 285].

Moving into the midphase, in terms of theory development, few would now object to Loewald's closing remarks:

On the analyst's side, his responsiveness to each patient is a new rendition, shaped by the patient's transference, of his specially trained ability to use his own love—hate in the service of analyzing. Observing and understanding the patient analytically and conveying this understanding to him by interpretive interventions, is the analyst's enactment of his caring for another person [p. 286].

What we see now is a two-person psychology, still focused one one analysis, wherein, as in infant development, the self-as-given evolves through becoming attuned to its significant others and through eliciting reciprocal attunements. In the psychoanalytic situation, self and other intermix, blend properties, coalesce, retool, and reestablish their separate domains.

Friedman's Paradox

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

450 N. Woodward Avenue
Birmingham, MI 48009

Melvin Bornstein  

The title of Dr. Friedman's book is a little misleading, for his subject is really about psychoanalysis and psychoanalysts. I suspect he decided to use the term psychotherapy in its most literal sense, not as a mode of treatment, and what he is anatomizing is the psychoanalytic process. One can, with impunity, substitute psychoanalysis as one reads because all his source material, as well as his stance, is psychoanalytic.

What is a little unusual is that, in describing what he sees as the essentials of the psychoanalytic interaction, his lens remains trained on the analysis, rather than on the patient, especially the experience of the analyst. The reader will be more accurately oriented to the questions Dr. Friedman poses if he understands the author's aims and approach.

Dr. Friedman's book gives evidence of his having thought long and hard about the psychoanalytic treatment situation. His familiarity with what others have written about the subject is clear. His approach is essentially historical. He compensates for the absence of his own clinical material by illustrating points he wishes to make through the writings of his predecessors. This method is informative and illuminating but carries with it the same pitfalls that accompany using direct clinical data; for instead of drawing inferences from what a patient has said or done, Dr. Friedman draws inferences from what analysts have written.

Dr. Bornstein is Training and Supervising Analyst, Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.

Psychotherapy Versus Psychoanalysis: A Theory-Dependent Distinction?

Estelle Shane PHD and Morton Shane MD

Morton Shane

1800 Fairburn Avenue
Suite 203
Los Angeles, CA 90025

Morton Shane  

It goes without saying, almost, especially in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry inspired by his contributions, that Lawrence Friedman has created an outstanding collection of psychoanalytic-psychotherapeutic essays, one that any clinician in the field must admire and be grateful for. His mastery of the history of psychoanalytic thought is superb, informed as it is by his own original synthesis and by insights of remarkable clarity. In the face of such perceptiveness, where so many questions of central importance have been addressed with so much subtlety and finesse, we are left with one disappointment: Why hasn't this powerful mind solved for us a seemingly simple conundrum confronting psychoanalysis ever since early in the century, when Freud first commented upon the reverse alchemy of transmuting the pure gold of psychoanalysis into it baser alloy, psychotherapy? Why hasn't Friedman, in other words, more effectively distinguished between psychoanalysis and the psychotherapy that serves as the subject for his many unique and penetrating contributions?

Estelle Shane, Ph.D., is Copresident, Training and Supervising Analyst, Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis; Training and Supervising Analyst, Los Angeles Psychoanalytic Society and Institute; and Assistant Professor of Psychiatry, University of California, Los Angeles.

Morton Shane, M.D., is Copresident, Training and Supervising Analyst, Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis; Training and Supervising Analyst, Los Angeles Psychoanalytic Society and Institute; and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of California, Los Angeles.

Epilogue

Newell Fischer Issue Editor and Ruth Fischer Issue Editor

Ruth Fischer

Ruth Fischer  

In reviewing our contributions, it is possible to focus either on the common ground or on the areas of diversity. Both perspectives are important. Looking for areas of agreement will disclose central components in the therapeutic process, whereas underscoring diversity will shed light on new avenues for exploration and further elaboration.

Michels (1985), in discussing the therapeutic action of psychoanalysis, delineates three primary themes that have been put forward to account for the therapeutic efficacy of psychoanalysis. In underscoring these components, he is careful to emphasize that most psychoanalytic theoreticians include all these elements in their view of the therapeutic process, but they emphasize one or another of them. The first of these themes is the attainment of insight—the analysand discovers something new about himself and/or sees what is old in a new way. This category includes Freud's therapeutic goal of making conscious that which is unconscious, efforts at reconstructing pathogenic forces, and the development of a meaningful life narrative. Theoreticians partial to this school of thought see enhancing self-knowledge as critical in producing therapeutic change. The second theme focuses on the experience of an intense emotional encounter. In the psychoanalytic arena this is not simply an issue of catharsis, but rather a gradually evolving affective experience that is felt to be critical in producing change. Finally is the emphasis on an interpersonal experience. The relationship between analysand and analyst is considered the central and dominant curative component.

Again, it is important to emphasize that most theories of cure would include all three of these elements. However, there is considerable debate as to which dominates and which remain important background factors in accounting for therapeutic efficacy.

Using this simplified schema, the common ground of the presentations is that our contributors would certainly include all three elements.

Prologue

Eloise Agger D.S.W.

Eloise Agger

Eloise Agger  

In “how the Analyst's work shapes the analyst—i” (Psychoanalytic Inquiry, Volume 13, Number 3, 1993), we were privileged to meet, in turn, the minds of six analysts and to ponder the forces that shape them. Four men and two women led us into their private consultation rooms. The question addressed therein was what analyzing does to the analyst. While it is clear that theory informs technique, one might ask, as I did in the Prologue in 1993, “how does the work we do influence us, shape our theory, modify our attitudes and personality, influence our behavior, affect the quality of our subjective states, and leave its mark on the inner reaches of our selves?”

A common thread running through the material presented then, and in the six essays that follow, is of the analyst as a participant observer, learning about him- or herself while regressing in the service of the other. In fact, one measure of the analyst's degree of maturation could be said to depend on the extent to which there exists within him or her a growing capacity to actively engage in constructive encounters within an empathically attuned analytic space. Another common thread is the idea that the formulation of a psychoanalytic interpretation begins in the analyst's subjective experience of what it “feels” like to be with that particular other self (or aspect of self) during a specific moment of contact and then to reshape that experience within a frame of cognitive meaning.

Leo Rangell (1993), commenting on these premises in another context, validates the idea of the analyst's being affected by his work and then raises useful questions. “No clinician working for any length of time fails to register an appreciation of the occupational accomplishments (rewards and complications) of analyzing. Every hour, every day, every year accumulates its identifications, counter-experiences, approaches to anxiety, or sorties over the border, and the defenses and maneuvers away from these, on the parts of analysts in their daily work….

Prologue

Newell Fischer Issue Editor and Ruth Fischer Issue Editor

Ruth Fischer

Ruth Fischer  

In keeping with the spirit of this journal as epitomized by its name, Psychoanalytic Inquiry, we present in this issue responses to an inquiry of our own. What, we asked the participating authors, from your work within the psychoanalytic process or experience leads to cure, or more modestly stated, what fosters psychic growth and improvement? It is important to note this is but one of a cluster of related questions. We have not addressed the issue of whether psychoanalysis cures and what the data are, a not insignificant issue in the current political economic climate. Nor have we addressed the nature of “cure” or the nature of change in the psychoanalytic encounter. Our aim is a better understanding of the therapeutic action of the psychoanalytic process.

At a different level of inquiry, we wonder why it is that the question of the curative element in psychoanalysis has been repeatedly raised. As analysts, our preoccupation with this line of inquiry goes back over 100 years to Freud's Preliminary Communications (1893). The conference at Marienbad in 1936 and the series of panels at the scientific meetings of the American Psychoanalytic Association and at the International Psychoanalytical Association are a small, but representative, sample of the ongoing discourse related to this topic. In 1989, Psychoanalytic Inquiry devoted an issue to “Change and Therapeutic Effectiveness in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy,” edited by Pietro Castelnuovo-Tedesco. The focus there was similar to the one now being considered. The literature examining the nature of the psychoanalytic process and studying the essential and curative elements in the analytic endeavor is extraordinarily rich and diverse. A review of it is tantamount to surveying 100 years of psychoanalytic thinking. (Cooper's 1989 historical survey is a good starting point for such an overview.) The attention this subject has received over the years attests to the priority it has taken in our thinking.

[[RunningHead]]

It Is All Interaction

Arnold Goldberg MD

Arnold Goldberg

Arnold Goldberg  

Somewhere between viewing the analyst as detached observer and informed interpreter of the analysand's associations and viewing the analyst as active participant in the patient's psychic life, there lies a truth about the nature and degree of analyst-patient interaction. In another sense, however, there is a very certain participation of the analyst in every patient's psychology. Perhaps this lies at a different level from whatever the analyst may or may not do; that is, it is beyond overt interaction. It comes from the fact that inaction may count as much as action, silence as much as talking, and understanding as much as misunderstanding. There is no certain path to neutrality and/or nonparticipation, since the proper stance of an analyst is always to be able to be surprised at the results of his or her presence as well as behavior. Everything seems to matter, and so interaction needs to be considered along a spectrum of accidental to intentional, as well as incidental to meaningful.

If we assume that the patient always has an effect on the analyst and that the same holds true for that of the analyst upon the patient, then we need to clarify both the nature of the proper constraints of an analysis and how to manage and explain this inevitable mutuality of interaction. As to the first, it is clear that we evoke moral and ethical limits to analyst-patient interaction. We likewise insist upon actions or restraints that facilitate treatment. We abstain from physical contact, both because we feel it improper and because it impedes the treatment.

Dr. Goldberg is Training and Supervising Analyst, Institute for Psychoanalysis, Chicago; and Professor of Psychiatry, Rush Medical College.

Psychoanalytic Interaction

Jay Greenberg PHD

Jay Greenberg

275 Central Park West, 1BB
New York, NY 10024

Jay Greenberg  

A middle-aged professional man arrives for his analytic session, lies down on the couch, and immediately announces, “My mind is blank.” It is something this patient does frequently; although the symptoms for which he sought help have improved dramatically since he began treatment a year and a half ago, he has never particularly enjoyed or trusted the process.

I know, because it has happened often before, that Mr. C becomes anxious when he has no agenda. Free association is not his cup of tea; it requires that he open himself receptively, and this is anathema to a man whose character is largely organized around expunging all vestiges of anything he might think of as passive or feminine. But today, I am not quite sure why, I know that Mr. C is not simply describing a state of mind; there is something of an incantation in his words. He is not just telling me how he feels; he is also warning me about what the next forty-five minutes will be like for both of us.

The statement quickly affects my mood; I begin to worry about getting through the hour with my own spirits intact. I can feel myself withdrawing; paying attention to Mr. C is becoming difficult. It seems as if my mind could easily become as blank as his, not the blankness of evenly hovering attention with its promise of discovery around every corner, but the blankness of despair.

Dr. Greenberg is Editor, Contemporary Psychoanalysis; Training and Supervising Analyst, William Alanson White Institute; Faculty and Supervising Analyst, Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis, New York University.

Presented as part of the panel “Toward a Definition of the Term and Concept of Interaction,” at the winter meeting of the American Psychoanalytic Association, New York, NY, December 21, 1991.

Discussion

Arnold Richards MD

Arnold Richards

200 East 89th Street
Suite 45C
New York, NY 10128

Arnold Richards  

This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry on the topic of interaction provides both a challenge and an opportunity for a discussant. The challenge is to illuminate a concept that is au courant but hard to grasp. The opportunity is to use the various commentaries on interaction as the basis for a wide-ranging discussion of the nature of psychoanalytic theory and clinical practice.

In what follows, I will define and sharpen the disagreement among the contributors, but I will also attempt to identify the basis for integration of certain viewpoints that only appear to be disparate. Let me record at the outset my general impression that, in addressing the notion of interaction, the contributors to this issue felt they were sailing in uncharted waters. Thus, each contributor turned to theories and concepts with which he or she felt at home: Meissner focused on empathy and the therapeutic alliance; Schwaber on the listening process; Sandler on the idea of the representational world; Oremland on relational matrices; Goldberg on issues of connection and self-objects; Hurst on the problem of abstinence; and Lichtenberg on the data of infant observation and infant-caregiver interaction.

Meissner's paper focuses less on analysis as a data-gathering process than on the curative process per se. His effort is to define the relationships among empathy, therapeutic alliance, transference, data gathering, and cure.

Dr. Richards is Training and Supervising Analyst, New York Psychoanalytic Institute; Faculty, New York Psychoanalytic Institute; Editor, Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association.

Fred Hilkert  

Lawrence friedman has included a number of his previously published papers in a book that dissects the therapist's experience of psychotherapy. He argues that stress and theory comprise that experience, with stress obscured in theory and theory performing the treatment. The theory he refers to is psychoanalytic theory, but the application he seeks is to dynamic psychotherapy as well as to psychoanalysis.

Friedman is a physician in his early 60s. During his psychiatric residency, he taught philosophy. He is now Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at Cornell Medical School (APA Biographical Directory, 1989; Biographical Directory of the APA, 1977). Friedman regards much of psychoanalytic theory from the vantage point afforded by philosophy. He is a member of an illustrious company in psychoanalysis who have benefited from the rigors of that discipline. In addition, he adds a historic perspective from the evolvement of nineteenth century thought that reveals the ideational foundations upon which psychoanalysis was built. He is a member of the editorial board of Psychoanalytic Quarterly.

Discussion on The Anatomy of Psychotherapy

Robert Michels MD

Robert Michels

525 East 68th Street, Box 170
NY, NY 10021

Robert Michels  

Larry Friedman's book, The Anatomy of Psychotherapy, is brilliant. It sparkles with insight into what psychotherapy is about, what makes it different from other human relationships, and, particularly, the role that theory plays in making psychotherapy unique. He outlines his argument early in his presentation. Therapists, he tells us, are always uncomfortable while doing therapy. They “function in a sea of trouble” (p. 6) and sit “in a broth of interpersonal pressures” (p. 6). They need help, and the treatment for their distress is provided by their theories. Psychoanalysis is described as the prototype theory of psychotherapists, and Friedman examines psychoanalysis, as well as a number of competing theories and dissenting psychoanalytic schools, in order to explore how theories work, how therapists use them, and, particularly, the specific ways in which different theories come to the assistance of the ever uncomfortable therapist, facilitating or inhibiting the therapy in the process.

This is by no means a textbook of psychotherapy, and a beginning student of psychotherapy would best avoid it. However, it is similar to such a text in that it is about people with problems (in this case therapists rather than patients) and the strategies that are employed in solving those problems (in this case theories rather than psychotherapy). Therefore, it is interesting to compare it to such a textbook.

Dr. Michels is The Walsh McDermott Professor of Medicine, Professor of Psychiatry, Cornell University Medical College, and Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.

Abstinence and Interaction

David Hurst MD

David Hurst

601 Emerson Street
Denver, CO 80218

David Hurst  

More interaction between analyst and patient in psychoanalysis has been advocated since 1925 (Ferenczi and Rank, 1925), but judging by the literature, most analysts abstain from interacting with patients beyond observing, questioning, and interpreting.

I make three points in this paper: (1) Strict adherence to the principle of abstinence makes an analyst wary of interacting with her or his patients; (2) the meaning of abstinence should be revised from drive-discharge terms to the terms of contemporary analytic technique; (3) some of the most effective analysis is done following a conscious suspension or an unconscious lapse of abstinence that leads to an enactment of the transference-countertransference relationship. A case is described to illustrate this final point.

Abstinence is a sine qua non of psychoanalytic technique, permitting analyst and patient to explore overstimulating memories and fantasies by controlling the risk of acting them out, analogous to the way the neurologic inhibition of movement in the dream state protects the dreamer.

Originally proposed by Freud (1915) to prevent overgratification of the libidinal transference, abstinence can be more relevantly described today. We no longer abstain from overgratifying the transference for reasons of drive discharge, but because the playing out and interpretation of unconscious fantasy must be done against a background of containment and reflection in order to maintain the safety of the psychoanalytic situation.

Dr. Hurst is Training and Supervising Analyst, Denver Institute for Psychoanalysis; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of Colorado School of Medicine.

J. Burland MD

J. Burland

15 Colwyn Lane
Bala-Cynwyd, PA 19004

J. Burland  

To identify this presentation with the label “developmentalist” is to attempt to indicate some significant difference from “non-developmentalists.” I would like to start, however, by outlining what I feel to be similarities between this developmentalist's understanding of psychoanalytic cure and that of the vast majority of psychoanalysts, including those who do not label themselves “developmentalists.”

The Psychoanalytic Process

The psychoanalytic process is shaped not by our theories, but by the nature of the human mind. How psychoanalysts understand the human mind determines, therefore, how they understand the psychoanalytic process. There are a set of basic psychoanalytic hypotheses concerning the mind that are shared by almost all psychoanalysts, which is associated with a shared view of the psychoanalytic process.

Memorial to Michael Franz Basch

Joseph Lichtenberg Editor-in-Chief

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Our colleague, friend, and fellow editor, Michael Franz Basch, died on January 28, 1996. All who knew Mike were shocked by the suddenness and untimeliness of his leaving us. But then Mike had always seemed to be in an admirable time warp. With his more formal style of dress and gentlemanly manner, he seemed to embody the aristocratic culture of a cherished Europe of a bygone era. Yet Mike was very present. He fully appreciated the implications of the findings of contemporary research in affects, infant development, and neurophysiology. By any standard, Mike had a brilliant mind. Remarkably erudite, he was also able to do what only a few true intellectuals can—he could communicate in a simple, direct, and precise manner in his superb writing and lecturing on psychotherapy. Psychoanalytic Inquiry rejoices that he was one of our editors from our inception.

Howard Levine MD

Howard Levine

124 Dean Road
Brookline, MA 02146

Howard Levine  

You might say that a therapist “does” an interpretation on his patient to make him react some way.

Friedman, 1988 (p. 139)

Consider the following situation: Two people contract to do something together, with one well aware that what the other seeks is neither fully known nor knowable in the beginning and, in either case, not at all what he or she intends to provide. I am, of course, describing the analyst and analysand and the radical differences that inevitably arise between their various goals for the treatment. The tensions that develop as their dysjunction of aims becomes increasingly apparent will help drive the process of the analysis. Indeed, in one sense, these tensions will contribute to the very sum and substance of what is to be analyzed—the transference neurosis. The fact that the analytic situation is constructed in just this way—to activate in analyst and analysand the very wishes that the analyst will attempt to refuse to gratify—leads both participants into the labyrinth of frustrated desire that has helped earn psychoanalysis the reputation of being “the impossible profession.

A Note on the Psychoanalytic Process: The Analysand's Contribution

Newell Fischer MD

Newell Fischer

111 North 49th Street
Philadelphia, PA 19139

Newell Fischer  

My effort in this essay on what “cures” in psychoanalysis is to underscore the patient's impact on the therapeutic process. Whereas the focus in the literature concerning the analytic encounter has largely been on the role and the specific theoretical frame of the analyst, the contribution of the patient in shaping the psychoanalytic engagement is either taken for granted or considered of lesser significance. From this perspective, the skills, personality style, theoretical “school,” and the specific interventions of the analyst are highlighted and considered fundamental to the particular qualities of the unfolding analytic process. To add some balance to this view, I am suggesting that, in a complex and interactive way, the analysand's character structure, inner conflicts, and psychopathology profoundly shape the analytic process and to a large degree determine the unique “mix” of what “cures” in the analytic arena.

To place my comments in context, it is important to note that any discussion that attempts to separate out and examine one sector of a complex, multifactorial and interactive process carries with it the hazard of oversimplification, reductionism, and inevitably, a degree of distortion. In such a discussion, it is quite clear that the selective attention must relegate to the background other important factors, as well as put aside those components introduced by the dynamics of simultaneity and mutual interaction.

Dr. Fischer is Executive Director, Training and Supervising Analyst, The Philadelphia Psychoanalytic Institute; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of Pennsylvania; and Senior Attending Psychiatrist, Institute of Pennsylvania Hospital.

Commentary on The Anatomy of Psychotherapy

Theodore Jacobs MD

Theodore Jacobs

170 East 77th Street
Apt. 1G
New York, NY 10021

Theodore Jacobs  

Asked to assess the concert performances of the Rolling Stones, the pass rush of Lawrence Taylor of the Giants, or Boris Becker's powerful first serve, the adolescent of today is likely to respond with a single descriptive word: awesome.

To my mind, Lawrence Friedman is in a class with the Stones, with Lawrence Taylor, and with Boris Becker. His book The Anatomy of Psychotherapy is truly awesome. Bringing together work that Dr. Friedman has done during the past two decades, as well as new contributions, it mixes wit, wisdom, scholarship, and penetrating criticism with the insights of a philosopher and a historian to produce a truly remarkable volume.

In fact, although contained within one cover, Dr. Friedman's work is actually more than one book. It consists of several sections that may be viewed as separate monographs, each instructive, each informative. Perhaps the most notable contribution is Dr. Friedman's memorable work on the theory and practice of psychotherapy, a penetrating look at the belief system that informs the thinking of therapists and patients alike and a dissection of some of the unrecognized and little discussed needs that motivate much of the behavior of the two participants in the therapeutic encounter.

Dr. Jacobs is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Albert Einstein College of Medicine; Training and Supervising Analyst, New York Psychoanalytic Institute and Psychoanalytic Institute at New York University; and on the Editorial Board, The Psychoanalytic Quarterly.

The Patient Makes the Analyst

Neville Symington

Neville Symington

88 B, Warragal Road
Turramurra 2074
Sydney, NSW, Australia

Neville Symington  

I had finished my analysis. My two training cases had satisfied both my supervisors and the Education Committee of the British Society. So I was now qualified as a psychoanalyst. I had changed to an astonishing degree through the course of my analysis so I knew from personal experience that psychoanalysis is able to bring about profound psychological change. However, even when such an analysis does alter the inner emotional structure and intentional direction, it requires an agent from outside to summon that inner change into the outer forum. The patient I am about to describe was such an agent.

She came to see me after a frightening experience in which she saw herself merged with her mother and strangling her boyfriend. She had had some counselling in the provinces and then been assessed at a well-known clinic. She was then referred to the London Clinic for Psycho-Analysis, turned down there, and returned to the first clinic. Finally, she was referred to me when I was working at a little known clinic. She was angry at being shunted from pillar to post and disappointed not to have been taken on at the first clinic. Now, seeing me for an assessment, she felt this was the last resort. She was desperate, found me a bit severe, but felt she could work with me. We started just after the New Year, and between then and Easter, the treatment went along harmoniously. I thought naively that things would continue in such a vein. After that first break, the nature of the interaction between us changed dramatically.

Leo Rangell

456 N. Carmelina Avenue

Leo Rangell  

Summary

This paper is about “analytic” treatment, which is not limited to psychoanalysis. What constitutes “analytic” is described. Psychoanalysis, as differentiated from psychoanalytic psychotherapy, has been discussed at great length in an abundant literature. In this presentation, the border of interest being focussed upon is not centrally between those two approaches but the interface between analytic and supportive psychotherapies. Supportive therapy aims to restore the functioning of the patient's ego to its premorbid state before its decompensation and the development of symptoms, while analytic therapy, from analytic psychotherapy to psychoanalysis, has as its goal an improvement of ego functioning to a higher level than prior to the onset of symptoms. An acquisition of an analytic skill, or at least an acquaintanceship that leads to an interest in this, can occur to a slight degree with minimal analytic sessions or exposure, to a considerable degree with long-standing and consistent analytic psychotherapy, and to a maximum degree of which the patient is capable, with that analyst, in a psychoanalysis.

The Social Construction of Therapeutic Action

Donnel Stern PHD

Donnel Stern

24 East 82nd Street
New York, NY 10028

Donnel Stern  

Theories of therapeutic action are shaped by underlying conceptions of the aims or goals of treatment, and aims, in turn, reflect both explicit and implicit beliefs about what is possible in human relatedness and how it is most desirable to live. Such beliefs are values. They are statements about what is important in life. While it is not often recognized, then, theories of therapeutic action are not only laden with values, but actually assert them.

It goes without saying that no psychoanalyst sets out to decide questions of values for patients. The analysand's autonomy has always been paramount. But theories of change are rooted in values, whether we like it or not. The way a particular analyst thinks and works nudges the patient toward living in one way and not another. There is nothing wrong with that. It is simply a fact, inevitable and, therefore, unreasonable to condemn. And so, while psychoanalysts will and should struggle not to decide questions for patients, they frequently cannot avoid favoring one side of the patient's conflicts over others. The scale will be tipped one way or the other, ceaselessly and inconspicuously. The analyst's task changes from the attempt to maintain that perfect balance Anna Freud (1936)

Caregiver-Infant, Analyst-Analysand Exchanges: Models of Interaction

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

6256 Clearwood Road
Bethesda, MD 20817

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Interaction, like regulation, structure, motivation, and experience, is a term of such breadth that, without further delineation, it offers little to psychoanalysis. In this paper, I describe the approach I take to a number of topics that are at times subsumed under the rubric of interaction. Two groups of observations are easy to regard as interactions: caregiver-infant exchanges and analyst-analysand exchanges. Even used for these exchanges the term conveys an impression of an observer external to the exchange—one who observes, catalogues, and assigns meanings to (interprets) what caregiver and infant or analyst and analysand are doing with each other. Being, to a degree, outside the exchange can free the observer from the sway of a more intense subjective bias, but that is the rub. The key to observing the ebb and flow of caregiver-infant and analyst-analysand exchanges lies in the subjective cuing of one another by affective-cognitive communication. Outside the interaction we can see what the participants are doing, but we often can't see how each is cuing the other to do it. Inside the interaction we can feel the evocative effect of the other's cues and the responsive effect of our own motivation, but we often respond long before we can be reflective about it, and then we generally are reflective only to a limited degree.

Dr. Lichtenberg is Editor-in-Chief of Psychoanalytic Inquiry; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Georgetown University; Founding Member and Director of the Institute of Contemporary Psychotherapy.

Owen Renik MD

Owen Renik

244 Myrtle Street
San Francisco, CA 94109

Owen Renik  

Aburgeoning contemporary literature on self-analysis testifies to the crucial place in analytic technique occupied by the analyst's self-observations and his or her reflections upon them (e.g., Jacobs, 1991, McLaughlin, 1981; Poland, 1986). The prevalent view is increasingly of clinical psychoanalysis as a learning experience for the analyst, as well as the analysand. My own impression is that the mechanism of action of clinical psychoanalysis requires the analyst to engage in significant self-discovery in the course of conducting an analytic treatment if that treatment is to be successful, and my purpose in these remarks will be to explain and illustrate this view of the analytic process.

We regularly observe that progressive analytic work unfolds via mutual active embroilment between analyst and analysand and through continuous effort on the part of both to become aware of and clarify the nature of the embroilment. Gradually, we have come to consider that the bilaterality of the personal entanglement that characterizes the analytic treatment relationship is not a regrettable consequence of the analyst's fallibility but, rather, a sine qua non, of the psychoanalytic process. Boesky (1990), for example, concludes, “If the analyst does not get emotionally involved sooner or later in a manner that he had not intended, the analysis will not proceed to a successful termination” (p. 573). Bird (1972)

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Our contributors have brought us closer to a clearer conceptualization of interaction within psychoanalysis. Without exception, they emphasize the necessity of viewing interaction from an intrapsychic perspective, which reflects the current trend to understand interaction as signifying more than the interpersonal/social. Each contributor, with varying degrees of emphasis, supports Schwaber's insistence that, for interaction to be considered analytic, it must be considered in terms of experience. The difference seems to revolve on the emphasis placed on whether interaction is considered from the standpoint of a one-person or a two-person model.

Yet, as Gill and Richards point out in their discussions, even Schwaber and Goldberg, who emphasize a one-person model perspective of interaction, leave room for consideration of the analyst's psychic activity in the analytic process.

In his final statement on the one-person-two-person dilemma, Gill provides us with his own evocative view. He suggests finding a place for interaction in our psychoanalytic lexicon by viewing it in terms of a complementary series of the innate/intrapsychic and the experiential/intrapsychic.

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

For the last three decades, Lawrence Friedman has given psychoanalysts a fresh slant on the analytic situation. He has written of the experience of the analyst, which, until recently, was uncommon in analytic literature. He has asked how analysts think in the analytic situation. What are their sources of gratification and frustration? How do they deal with their frustration? How do their needs correspond and diverge from their patients' needs? By understanding why analysts use theory, he explores the experience of the analyst, the reasons that analysts use a particular theory, and the evolution of theory in response to the changing needs of the analyst.

Lawrence Friedman is ideally suited for this task. He is trained in philosophy, history, and psychiatry. His understanding of psychoanalysis is extensive. His writings have special relevance for psychoanalysis because of the current attention given to the experience of the analyst in the analytic situation.

Although the title The Anatomy of Psychotherapy refers to psychotherapy, the book is actually about psychoanalysis. Friedman's premise is that psychoanalysis is a stressful encounter. He believes that it is stressful because of the demands it evokes from the patient, which will be frustrated, and the unnatural responses to the patient's demands that are required of the analyst. The analyst turns to theory for guidance and support in this unnatural situation.

Friedman contends that the objectives of analysis are different for the analyst and patient. The patient wants relief from discomfort and attempts to influence the analyst to provide him with that relief. The analyst wants to analyze and feel like an analyst. In the ideal analytic situation, the analyst remains ambiguous and avoids influencing the patient. The disparity in objectives comprises a major paradox in the psychoanalytic situation. Throughout his book, Friedman deals with how analysts have grappled with that paradox.

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

In Friedman's response to the papers in this issue, he clarifies his arguments. His entrance to analysis is an exploration of how analysts use theory. It is not an exploration of the function of theory in helping us understand the world. It is not an attempt to develop a theory of the analyst. Although he recognizes that the analyst has many motivations that are expressed in the therapeutic situation, like helping patients and making money, these motivations do not define the analytic situation. The fundamental enterprise of psychoanalysis is to create change in a socially awkward and ambiguous situation that invites discomfort.

Although each contributor to the issue has questioned Friedman's fundamental premise of the analyst's use of theory to reduce the stress intrinsic to the analytic situation, each contributor believes that Friedman is one of the important psychoanalytic thinkers of our time. His importance rests in his ability to make us think about the clinical situation in new ways with different words and concepts.

Jerusalem 93223 Israel

Rivka Eifermann  

Omitting—The Problem, the Issue

Writing on the topic of this issue, “how analytic work shapes the analyst,” presents a problem that is at the heart of all analytic writing. The issue is an invitation to analysts to write about their work and personal experiences. We are not free to fully report on our patients, nor do we feel free or willing to report fully on ourselves. My purpose herein is to examine some implications of these limitations in public self-reporting, taking as an example an instance of omission in my own writing regarding my self-analysis, and describing how the eventual inclusion of the omitted aspect in the present paper interelates with my work with patients. Some more general ramifications of the prevalent exclusion of self-analysis from public discourse—with the exception of countertransference—are discussed with regard to the biases such partial reporting may introduce in our psychoanalytic thinking and practice.

Matters laboriously uncovered in our analytic and self-analytic engagements in search of truth are often covered up in our writing.

Rivka R. Eifermann is Supervising and Training Analyst at the Israel Psychoanalytic Society and its past president; on the teaching staff of the Society's Institute; and Associate Professor on the Faculty of the Psychology Department of The Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Ultimately, everything in psychoanalysis can be reduced to interaction. Our major concepts, formulations, models, and strategies are derived from the interaction between the analyst and the patient in the analytic relationship. The profound psychic experiences of the analyst and the patient are a result of their mutual interaction. Both the Random House Unabridged and Webster's Second Edition define interaction as reciprocal action or influence. The humanistic core of psychoanalysis rests upon this definition.

Yet the meaning of interaction used in psychoanalytic discourse has been highly ambiguous. The term does not even appear in any of Freud's works. Transference and countertransference do, yes, but always in terms of a one-person model, either the patient—mostly the patient—or the analyst. During the forties and fifties the term interaction gradually began to appear in the analytic literature, but only in reference to the extrapsychic interpersonal dimension. Interaction was relegated to the descriptive, the behavioral. It was nonanalytic and frequently used pejoratively in connection with the Sullivanian interpersonal model. We have since come a long way.

Until the 1960s, we faced a paradoxical situation: Although interaction was fundamental to psychoanalysis, the word was not in our lexicon, and the concept was alien to our theory. It was not, however, alien to our practice. Psychoanalysts trained prior to the seventies have been frustrated and dissatisfied with discrepancies between what they were experiencing clinically and what they were being taught. They found themselves reacting strongly to their patients, in discouragingly sharp contrast to descriptions in the literature and what was publically expressed, which were devoid of any interactive depth. The analysts in these descriptions were cool, distant, uninvolved; they calmly offered interpretations that explained the workings of their patients' minds.

On the Foundations of Cure in Psychoanalysis

Mark Gehrie PHD

Mark Gehrie

180 North Michigan Avenue, Suite 2400
Chicago, IL 60601

Mark Gehrie  

There is now more than at any other time in the history of psychoanalysis a greater diversity of theories of cure and, indeed, in underlying conceptions of the nature and aims of the psychoanalytic process. But while theories of cure certainly provide the (often unrecognized) backdrop for the management of process in analysis, theories themselves are not the curative element; they must be translated into systems for understanding and programs for action in the psychoanalytic situation. The ultimate arbiter of any theoretical orientation is the effectiveness and appropriateness of its translation into a qualitatively meaningful curative environment, that is, into a clinical process that achieves a “curative” goal. In this paper, I will briefly review selected literature and then present two clinical vignettes that illustrate moments in the establishment of a curative process.

In Friedman's (1978) discussion of “Trends in the Psychoanalytic Theory of Treatment,” he notes that Freud (1913, 1914, 1919, 1926, 1937) considered three broad areas in the achievement of benefits in treatment: understanding, attachment, and integration. Much of the history of the debate on the “healing” or curative process involves the relative emphasis placed on one or another of these aspects. For Freud (1914), remembering, rather than repeating, was the fundamental goal, and in this service the patient “must find the courage to direct his attention to the phenomena of his illness” (p. 152).

Dr. Gehrie is Faculty, Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis.

This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry is titled “Interaction: Reflections on One- or Two-Person Psychology,” while the panel at which six of the papers herein, those by Goldberg, Greenberg, Oremland, Sandler, Schwaber, and Hurst, were presented, was titled “Toward a Definition of the Term and Concept of Interaction.” The present title seems to define the issue concerning interaction to be that of a choice between one-person and two-person models, whereas the original title does not. In fact, the subject being discussed in most of the papers was the subject of an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry of 1988 under the title “The Intrapsychic and Interpersonal Dimensions: An Unresolved Dilemma.”

I will divide my discussion into three parts. First, I will discuss rather briefly all the papers except Goldberg's and Schwaber's in the light of the usual understanding of the term interaction, which has come to refer to the mutual influence of analyst and analysand, in contrast to the view that the analyst is an essentially emotionally uninvolved examiner of the patient's psychic reality, except for the occasional inadvertent departures from this “neutrality” and “abstinence,” which are called countertransference. Concomitantly, a greater role is given to this external influence relative to the intrapsychic in the analytic situation. Second, I will discuss at greater length the papers of Goldberg and Schwaber.

The interactional perspective in psychoanalysis has gained increasing prominence and acceptance as integral to the therapeutic and theoretical consensus in the field. The problem on both levels centers around the difficulties in bringing the disparate perspectives together in a coherent form that allows the intrapsychic and interactional frameworks to be utilized in complementary and mutually reinforcing ways in clinical analytic work. One aspect of the problem relates to a clearer conceptualization of the interactional dimensions that contribute to the psychoanalytic interpersonal interaction and, thus, come into play in the psychoanalytic dialogue.

I have argued (Meissner, 1992) that the therapeutic relationship in psychoanalysis involves multiple components; at a minimum these would include transference (and its correlative countertransference), the real relationship, and the therapeutic alliance. These components are constantly present and mutually interactive dimensions of the therapeutic relationship, but for clarity of thinking and effectiveness of our theoretical assessment of the therapeutic process, they demand distinction and separate articulation (distinguir pour unir). The conclusion of this line of argument is that the therapeutic alliance is to be distinguished from both transference and the real relation; it involves a separate line of expression and development in the analytic process and brings into focus different aspects of the analytic interaction than do either transference or real relation.

This paper deals with considerations on visual stages and pictorial representations that emerge from acoustic perception. I shall examine some visual phenomena that I have observed arising in my own mind during analytical sessions.

If you want to know more … inquire from your own experiences … or turn to the poets [Freud, 1933, p. 135].

In a calm room, two people together.

Through reviewing the basic contributions to the theories of curative factors in dynamic psychoanalysis, I focused on seven factors that influence cure for which there is some clinical—quantitative evidence. These seven are the following: 1) the quality of the therapeutic alliance, 2) the correctness of the transference formulation, 3) the accuracy of the interpretations, 4) the quality of self understanding, 5) the changes in the transference pattern, 6) the degree of internalization of the gains, and 7) the level of mental health.

This clinical-quantitative review is an update and new integration of past ones, including Freud's papers on technique (1912, 1913); Knight (1949); Ekstein and Wallerstein (1958); Menninger and Holzman (1973); Luborsky (1984); Crits-Christoph, Mintz, and Auerbach (1988); Miller, Luborsky, Barber, and Docherty (1993); and Orlinsky, Grawe, and Parks (1994).

In recent years, there has been more attention to analysts' thoughts and behaviors within the analytic situation. In this paper, I will identify some of the ideas that shed light on the emotional reactions of the analyst to the patient. Because it is difficult to categorize the reactions of the analyst, my remarks are incomplete and heuristic in intention. My comments are divided into three categories: (1) prescribed attitudes for the analyst towards the analytic situation, (2) empirical descriptions of the analyst's reactions and how these descriptions have evolved over time. Here, I will cover reactions to the work with patients that are narrowly defined as countertransference or enactment, as well as general reactions of analysts to patients. I will include how the analyst's character structure shapes his reactions under the subheadings of Inside—Outside Paradox, Patient—Analyst Match, The Analytic Group, and Translations. I will give some further examples of empirical data that describe the complexity of the analytic interaction with a focus on the analyst's subjective feelings. (3) The last category is the development of the analyst, how it compares in contrast with theories of adult development concerning other professions.

Throughout this paper, I use the masculine gender for patient and analyst, except for the clinical vignette.

Patients seek psychoanalysis for many reasons—neurotic symptoms, psychosomatic conditions, relationship problems—yet in the final analysis, all the many reasons that bring people to psychoanalysis have to do with problems of the mind. Any definition of interaction poses the peril of being over-inclusive to the point that all meaning is lost. Defining interaction requires looking microscopically into the heart of relatedness.

In psychoanalysis interaction generally is used in two ways. Interaction refers to the composite interplay that takes place between the two participants of psychotherapy, and interaction refers to a class of interventions, a specific mode.

Interaction in the generic sense can be understood along innumerable lines that logarithmically increase as the transferences in interpersonal relationships are considered. Considering the variety of interacting introjects manifested in the flow of multiple transient and enduring regressions in the psychotherapeutic interplay, varyingly contributed to by each participant, intrapsychically, the interpersonal dyad is a crowd.

The Patient as Instrument of Change in the Analyst

Theodore Jacobs MD

Theodore Jacobs

170 East 77th Street, 1G
New York, NY 10021

Theodore Jacobs  

Change in the patient sometimes requires change in the analyst. When progress in an analysis has ended, when resistances appear unmodifiable, or when transferences on both sides of the couch interact to produce a stalemate, problems in the analyst often contribute in significant ways to the impasse that has developed. Sometimes, the difficulties arise from failures of understanding, sometimes from unrecognized transferences in the analyst, and sometimes from errors of technique.

Whatever the source of the problem, however, the prescribed remedies are familiar: consultation with colleagues, further supervision, or more personal analysis. While each of these methods has proven valuable in helping analysts overcome difficulties that have impinged on the treatment, they are ad hoc solutions that ultimately must be replaced by the analyst's ability to work with himself.

Each analyst develops his own style of self-scrutiny, aided by the unique stimulation of the analytic situation. The sustained exposure to powerful unconscious forces, both in his patient and in himself, which are integral parts of that situation, inevitably awakens those unresolved conflicts in the analyst that are tapped by the particular features of each treatment. As gadflies, rabble rousers, and disturbers of the peace, patients prick us, pull us, and sting us to look inward and to grapple anew old with ghosts newly awakened.

Dr. Jacobs is Clinical Professor, Albert Einstein College of Medicine; Training and Supervising Analyst, the New York Psychoanalytic Institute and the Psychoanalytic Institute at New York University.
